summary: Inheritance allows a child class to reuse code from a parent class, while polymorphism lets the same method name behave differently depending on the object calling it.
shortNotes: Inheritance uses the `extends` keyword so a subclass acquires fields and methods of its superclass.
Polymorphism means 'many forms' — one method name can produce different behaviour in different classes.
Method overriding lets a subclass provide its own version of a method already defined in the parent class.
The `super` keyword is used to call the parent class constructor or methods from the child class.
Runtime polymorphism is achieved through method overriding and a parent-type reference pointing to a child object.
Method overloading (same name, different parameters in the same class) is compile-time polymorphism.

detailed.explanation:
**Inheritance** is one of the four pillars of Object-Oriented Programming. It allows a new class (called a *subclass* or *child class*) to inherit the properties and behaviours of an existing class (called a *superclass* or *parent class*). This promotes code reuse. In Java, you write `class Dog extends Animal` to say that `Dog` is a type of `Animal` and automatically gets all non-private fields and methods of `Animal`.

The `super` keyword has two main uses in Java. First, `super()` inside a child class constructor calls the parent class constructor — Java actually does this automatically if you do not write it explicitly. Second, `super.methodName()` lets you call the parent version of an overridden method from inside the child class.

**Polymorphism** means the ability of a single interface (method name) to represent different underlying forms. There are two types in Java. *Compile-time polymorphism* (method overloading) happens when multiple methods share the same name but differ in the number or type of parameters, and the correct one is chosen at compile time. *Runtime polymorphism* (method overriding) happens when a parent-class reference variable holds a child-class object and the JVM decides at runtime which overridden method to call.

**Method Overriding** requires the method in the child class to have the exact same name, return type, and parameter list as in the parent class. You should use the `@Override` annotation — it is not mandatory, but it helps the compiler catch mistakes. A method marked `final` in the parent class cannot be overridden.

A classic real-world example: an `Animal` class has a `sound()` method. `Dog` overrides it to print `Woof` and `Cat` overrides it to print `Meow`. When you write `Animal a = new Dog();` and call `a.sound()`, Java runs the `Dog` version at runtime. This is the power of polymorphism — your code is flexible and extensible.

definitions.meaning: A mechanism where a child class acquires fields and methods of a parent class using the `extends` keyword.
The class whose properties and methods are inherited by another class.
The class that inherits from a superclass and can add new features or override existing ones.
The ability of one method name to behave differently based on the object or the parameters involved.
Providing a new implementation of a method in a subclass that already exists in the superclass with the same signature.
Defining multiple methods in the same class with the same name but different parameter lists.
A reference in a subclass used to call the parent class constructor or methods.
An optional but recommended annotation that tells the compiler the method is intentionally overriding a parent method.

points: Java supports single inheritance only — a class can extend only one class, but it can implement multiple interfaces.
All classes in Java implicitly extend the `Object` class if no other parent is specified.
Private members of the parent class are NOT inherited by the child class — they exist in memory but cannot be accessed directly.
For runtime polymorphism to work, you must use a parent-type reference: `Animal a = new Dog();`.
The `@Override` annotation is a best practice — it causes a compile error if you accidentally mis-spell the method name.
Constructor is never inherited; you must call `super()` explicitly if you need a parameterised parent constructor.
A `final` class cannot be extended, and a `final` method cannot be overridden.
Exam tip: overloading is resolved at compile time; overriding is resolved at runtime (dynamic dispatch).

codeExample.explanation:
Line 2-16: We define the parent class `Animal` with a `name` field, a constructor, a `sound()` method, and a `sleep()` method.
Line 19-28: `Dog` extends `Animal`. Its constructor calls `super(name)` to pass the name up to the `Animal` constructor. It overrides `sound()` to print 'Woof!'.
Line 31-40: `Cat` similarly extends `Animal` and overrides `sound()` to print 'Meow!'.
Line 43: `Main` is our driver class.
Line 46-47: We create `Animal`-type references but assign `Dog` and `Cat` objects to them. This is runtime polymorphism.
Line 49-50: When `a1.sound()` is called, Java sees the actual object is a `Dog` at runtime and runs `Dog`'s `sound()`. Similarly for `a2`.
Line 52-53: `sleep()` is not overridden, so the inherited `Animal` version runs for both.
Expected output:
Bruno says: Woof!
Whiskers says: Meow!
Bruno is sleeping.
Whiskers is sleeping.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to call `super(args)` in the child constructor when the parent has only a parameterised constructor — Java cannot auto-insert it and gives a compile error.
Confusing method overloading with method overriding: overloading changes the parameter list in the SAME class; overriding uses the EXACT same signature in a CHILD class.
Assuming private fields of the parent class are directly accessible in the child class — they are not; use public or protected getter methods instead.

questions.prompt: Which keyword is used in Java to establish inheritance between two classes?
questions.explanation: `extends` is the correct keyword. `implements` is used for interfaces, `super` is a reference to the parent class, and `inherits` does not exist in Java.
Even though the reference type is `Animal`, the actual object is `Dog`. At runtime, Java calls the overridden `Dog` version — this is runtime polymorphism.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about the `super` keyword is correct?
options: It creates a new instance of the parent class.
It can only be used in static methods.
It is used to call the parent class constructor or methods.
questions.explanation: `super()` calls the parent constructor and `super.method()` calls a parent method. It cannot be used in static methods and has nothing to do with creating instances.

questions.prompt: Which type of polymorphism is achieved by method overriding in Java?
questions.explanation: Method overriding is resolved at runtime by the JVM based on the actual object type, so it is called runtime polymorphism (also known as dynamic dispatch).

questions.prompt: How many classes can a Java class directly extend at the same time?
questions.explanation: Java supports only single inheritance for classes — a class can extend only one class. Multiple inheritance is supported through interfaces.

questions.prompt: What happens if you mark a method as `final` in the parent class?
options: The child class must override it.
The method cannot be overridden in any child class.
The method can only be called using `super`.
questions.explanation: A `final` method cannot be overridden in any subclass. If a child class tries to override it, a compile-time error occurs.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between method overloading and method overriding with one example each.
questions.answer: Method overloading means having multiple methods with the same name but different parameters within the same class — for example, `add(int a, int b)` and `add(double a, double b)` in the same class. Method overriding means a subclass redefines a method inherited from the parent class using the exact same signature — for example, a `Dog` class overriding the `sound()` method of `Animal`. Overloading is resolved at compile time; overriding is resolved at runtime.
questions.explanation: This tests conceptual clarity on two commonly confused terms. The key distinguishing points are: location (same class vs subclass) and resolution time (compile time vs runtime).

questions.prompt: Why is the `@Override` annotation recommended even though it is optional in Java?
questions.answer: The `@Override` annotation tells the compiler that you intend to override a parent method. If you accidentally mis-spell the method name or change the parameter list, the compiler will show an error instead of silently creating a new overloaded method. It improves code safety and readability.
questions.explanation: This tests understanding of best practices. Without @Override, a typo in the method name just creates a new unrelated method — a subtle bug that is hard to find.
There are 3 Dog objects (at index 0, 2, 3) and 1 Cat object (at index 1). When the loop runs, the Dog version prints 'Woof' 3 times and the Cat version prints 'Meow' once.

questions.prompt: Create a class `Shape` with a method `area()` that prints 'Area not defined'. Create two subclasses `Circle` and `Rectangle` that override `area()` to print 'Area of Circle' and 'Area of Rectangle' respectively. In `main`, create a `Shape` array containing one `Circle` and one `Rectangle` object and call `area()` on each using a loop.
questions.explanation: The `Shape` array holds parent-type references. At runtime, Java checks the actual object type for each element and calls the correct overridden `area()` method — this is runtime polymorphism in action. The loop cleanly demonstrates how one piece of code can handle multiple types.

steps.say: Welcome! Today we are learning about two of the most important ideas in Java: inheritance and polymorphism. Let us start with inheritance.
Think of a parent and a child. A child naturally gets many traits from the parent. In Java, a child class inherits fields and methods from a parent class.

write.content: Child class gets parent's fields and methods

steps.say: We use the extends keyword to set up this relationship. Here is the basic syntax.
Now we write a Dog class that extends Animal, meaning Dog is a type of Animal.
Dog automatically gets everything Animal has, so we write less code and reuse what already exists.

scenes.title: The super Keyword and Constructor Chaining

steps.say: When Dog has its own constructor, we use the super keyword to call the parent Animal constructor and pass values up the chain.
Inside the Dog constructor, we write super of name. This runs the Animal constructor with that name value.
The next line calls the parent constructor. Without this, Java cannot set up the Animal part of Dog properly.
You can also use super dot method name to call a parent method from inside the child class when you need the original behaviour.
Polymorphism means many forms. In Java, a child class can give its own version of a parent method. This is called method overriding.
Both Dog and Cat inherit from Animal. Animal has a sound method. Each child overrides it with its own behaviour.
In Dog, sound prints Woof. In Cat, sound prints Meow. Same method name, different results.
Always use the at-Override annotation above the method. It tells the compiler you are intentionally overriding and helps catch typos.
Now the really powerful part. We can use an Animal type reference to hold a Dog object. Java figures out the right method to call at runtime.
We declare a1 as type Animal but assign a new Dog object to it.
When we call a1 dot sound, Java sees the actual object is a Dog and runs the Dog version that prints Woof.
This means one variable of type Animal can work with any animal subclass. Your code becomes flexible and easy to extend.
Great work! Let us quickly recap what we covered today.
Inheritance uses extends so a child class reuses the parent class code.

write.content: extends = inherit parent fields and methods

steps.say: The super keyword calls the parent constructor or method from the child class.
Method overriding means the child gives its own version of a parent method, and at-Override helps avoid mistakes.
Runtime polymorphism lets a parent reference hold a child object and call the correct overridden method at runtime. Practice these concepts with code and you will master them!
